prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms held at a magic wavelength allow many atoms to be interrogated at once and timekeeping to reach the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from B006 to B037. In round 1 I put the Higgs discovery first because it is a clue from nature, and I still think it is the most important result on the list. But a prize needs names, and six colleagues, including the particle physicist on the committee, have told me that the three-name leadership credit does not rest on a decisive discovery step. I proposed that credit myself as a compromise and nobody has produced the rationale that would turn it into more than that. B037 is the opposite case: a concrete invention, the magic-wavelength lattice that removes the light shift so that thousands of atoms can be interrogated at once, followed by a demonstration that took strontium clocks to the 10^-18 level, reproduced and intercompared in Tokyo, Boulder, Paris, Braunschweig and elsewhere. Seven of eight members ranked it, all proposed the same two names, and nobody has raised a scientific objection. It is also more than a stopwatch. Millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, bounds on drifts of constants and many-body clock operation are measurements of nature, and the instrument is what makes them possible. That answers, for me, the distinction I drew in round 1 between a method and a discovery: here the method is the discovery channel. The two names divide cleanly, Katori for the concept and first lattice clock, Ye for taking it to the accuracy and coherence frontier. I would ask that the citation be tied to the magic-wavelength lattice and to ensemble interrogation, and say nothing about the redefinition of the second, which has not happened and should not drive the wording.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 1997 laser-cooling, 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes is real. If the committee reads the lattice clock as an evolutionary refinement of those, then B037 is an excellent engineering achievement that does not belong in this prize. I think the many-atom, magic-wavelength regime is a distinct step, but I am a string theorist and I am relying on my atomic-physics colleagues for that judgement. The priority history is also unverified: Lindroth recalls it from memory, Kroll and Mehlig have not checked it, and I certainly have not. Paris (Lemonde, Le Targat), Boulder and NIST contributors, and the Al+ and other ion-clock groups have real claims that two names compress. No new physics has yet been seen with these clocks. If an expert report from the primary papers showed that the decisive steps were shared differently, I would want to revisit the credit rather than defend two names out of habit.

responses.point: Kroll would not rank the Higgs entry above the clock on the present attribution evidence, and would need a convincing answer on Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang before ranking B042 above B037. He also notes that no new physics has been seen with the clocks.
responses.response: I accept your Higgs point. If the committee would have to say publicly that the prize honours detector programmes while the citation reads as discovery, I do not think I can give you a defensible rationale, and I withdraw B006 as my first choice. On the clocks, you are right that nothing beyond the Standard Model has appeared, but the redshift across a millimetre, the constant-variation limits and the spin-squeezed operation are measurements nature could have answered differently, so I now regard the instrument as the experiment. I share your concern about B042 and BHZ; the committee should not rank it above B037 until the citation can be drafted without attributing the HgTe proposal to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp.

responses.point: Pearce, who has built detectors, argues that spokespersons and founding leaders are the weakest kind of credit and that the discovery rests on the analyses, the trigger, the calorimeters and the tracker, while the clock rests on calibration, systematics and independent confirmation. He asks that the priority history be checked by atomic-physics colleagues or an expert review.
responses.response: You put your finger on what I could not answer, and coming from someone who has worked inside such collaborations it carries more weight than my own view of the Higgs. I agree on the evidence standard as well: the clock result is trustworthy because several groups reproduce it and compare it. As Secretary I would insist that nothing be balloted on B037 until Lindroth, Johansson and Kroll, or an external referee, have set out the priority of Katori's proposal, the first strontium clock and Ye's accuracy work from the primary papers. That check is the condition on which my support rests, not a formality. Your own first choice, B003, I keep as nothing more than a respected neighbour, since it has the same difficulty of splitting the satellite and ground-based follow-up credit.

responses.point: Lindroth prefers B037, states the overlap with 2005 and 2012 as the main reservation, asks how broad the citation should be, and says she is recalling the magic-wavelength priority history from memory and may be inflating her judgement by familiarity. She would also keep B006 as an alternative if the citation honoured conception and construction of the detectors.
responses.response: I take your candour about familiarity seriously and think it argues for an external check, not against the candidate. On the breadth question I side with you and Johansson: widening the citation to optical clocks in general would pull in the ion-clock community and blur precisely the distinction that makes B037 clean, so the wording should stay with the magic-wavelength lattice. I note your offer on B006, to accept a citation that honours conception and construction of the detectors. I considered it, but I think that wording would be a different prize from the one my round-1 text claimed, and still leaves out thousands who built the experiments, so I leave B006 as a second alternative only.

responses.point: Eriksson defends B042 as an identifiable pair, the Z2 invariant and the HgTe observation, that does not depend on who else deserves mention, and says the credit omissions are a smaller problem than the leadership attribution of B006.
responses.response: That is a fair comparison, and I agree that B042 is better off than B006 on attribution: the names correspond to the original idea and the first experiment. I still hold to the concern I had in round 1, that the HgTe platform came from Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and that Zhang's death makes the record harder to balance. The 2016 prize also makes me ask what is new, though your Z2 argument is a real answer. I would be content with B042 as a fallback, which is why it is my first alternative, but I put B037 ahead because its credit has fewer open questions and its confirmation is broader.

responses.point: Johansson moved her preferred configuration to B037, citing its clean two-person credit, reproduction across laboratories and species, and the absence of scientific objections, and said she would reconsider B006 only if a defensible rationale for the three names were shown.
responses.response: Your position is close to mine now, and I thank you for stating the demand on B006 so clearly: no one, including me, has shown the rationale. I agree with your reading of the two credits, and I also accept your remark that part of the case is prospective. Where we may differ slightly is on timing: I would not let the coming redefinition of the second push the committee to decide early, and I would let the physics, already achieved, carry the prize. I also respect your decision to treat circuit QED with caution because of your closeness to that community.

uncertainties: Whether Katori and Ye have the right separable priority from the primary papers, against the Paris, Boulder and NIST contributors, and whether two names are sufficient.
Whether the committee will judge the lattice clock a distinct regime beyond the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, a judgement I make mainly on my colleagues' testimony.

Whether B042 can be worded so that Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, the 3D work and the quantum anomalous Hall effect are not attributed to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, which would change how I order B042 and B037.
Whether the Higgs experimental discovery can ever be given a defensible three-name credit under the statute, or whether it will remain the unrecognised half of the 2013 prize.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict has appeared for any shortlisted candidate. My ties to David Gross, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala string group do not touch the lattice clock, topological insulator or Higgs entries. I have not collaborated with Katori or Ye, and I am not an atomic physicist, so I rely on colleagues for the AMO judgement. My earlier first-place ranking of B006 was a scientific-importance judgement and is not a personal tie.
